title: Data and Security Responsibilities of the Individual Humanitarian
html:
Data and Security Responsibilities of the Individual Humanitarian

When thinking about the importance, and potential sensitivity, of humanitarian data, where should the responsibility of keeping it safe lie? With the organization or with the individual humanitarian? Of course, it needs to be some combination of both especially when field-based responders need to “get things done” (read: work around HQ-mandated restrictions). So, how can we find the right balance when attacks are ever increasing?* That is the question I posed to Lidewij Heerkens when she joined me mid last year.

We found the usual things. Like lack of donor funding - let’s be honest, it is not nearly as exciting to fund data or cyber security projects when compared to an innovation project. Or, gravely outdated information policies - some predating the iPhone. Or, the heavy reliance on staff to simply do the right thing even when faced with impossible scenarios. Or, proactive employees who self-pay for security solutions. The current responsibility put on the individual employee is a heavy burden, especially with limited training and support to implement protocols

Not to completely despair. There are positive actions being taken. Guidance and policy like the IASC’s Operational Guidance on Data Responsibility and the Centre for Humanitarian Data’s Guidance Note on The Implications of Cyber Threats for Humanitarians are helping to raise awareness. Micro-trainings at the Red Cross have seen incredibly high engagement and completion rate when compared to traditional, hour-long online security courses. And, practices - like scenario and impact analysis - are starting to make their way into our sector.

Consistency is key when it comes to data security. And, that is where the organization will need to put its effort - to make practice consistent while adaptable to the local situation. Other recommendations that we have outlined:

  • Targeted education. Training used to be “one-and-done”. Although this is changing, there is still work to be done.
  • Reward good behaviour.
  • Minimize the individual responsibility. Organization need to work on standardization, automation and role-based access.
  • Do not collect data that is not really needed
  • Scenario and impact analysis of data. The scenario analysis challenges employees to think about the potential impact in multiple scenarios. The analysis should become part of employees’ habits. What could happen if you lose control over your data? Think of it from a bad person’s perspective. 

Take a deeper look in our paper: Data and Security Responsibilities of the Individual Humanitarian

[PDF]

* In November 2022, Microsoft Digital Defence Reported noted that the volume of password attacks has soared to an estimated 921 attacks every second, a 74% rise in one year [PDF]
teaser: Who should keep humanitarian data safe, the organization or the individual? Research with Lidewij Heerkens on finding the balance.
